More importantly, the simple ratio of tree sizes is not sufficient to estimate productivity. Primary productivity corresponds to the increase in volume or biomass over a given time step. To calculate productivity, you therefore need to have data on the volume or above-ground biomass (AGB) of trees at two dates and calculate the difference, divided by the number of years between two measurements. ## Paper

## Abstract

Pathogens and herbivores are key to diversity-productivity relationships. However, the extent to
which plant diversity maintains higher productivity by reducing biomass loss from pathogens
and herbivores remains unclear at the global scale. Based on a meta-analysis of 2,315
observations from 316 studies, we show that, compared to monocultures, plant mixtures on
average reduce pathogens abundance and damage to plants by 30.1% and 31.7% and those of
invertebrate herbivores by 21.6% and 25.1%, while increasing plant productivity by 40.1% and
35.7%, respectively. Mixture effects on specialist pathogens and invertebrate herbivores become
more negative with increasing plant taxonomic, functional, and phylogenetic diversity in
mixtures, while those on generalist pathogens and i nvertebrate herbivores show no significant
relationships with any diversity metrics. Mixture effects on pathogens decrease with stand age
but those on invertebrate herbivores shift from negative to positive with stand age. Mixture
effects on pathogens and invertebrate herbivores are negatively associated with those on
productivity. Our findings highlight that conserving plant diversity could reduce biotic damage
to plants and enhance global primary productivity.

---

## Introduction

In the face of the continuous decline of plant diversity due to human activities,
understanding the relationship between biodiversity and ecosystem functions is critical for
optimizing management and conservation strategies 1,2. Biotic feedback from other trophic levels
(e.g. pathogens and herbivores) has been proposed to be a key mechanism for the biodiversity-
ecosystem productivity relationships 3. However, on a global scale, the effects of plant diversity
on pests and diseases as well as productivity may be highly dependent on the use of plant
diversity metrics, types of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores (i.e. fungal vs. bacteria; foliar
vs. soil vs. stem; specialists vs. generalists), stand age, ecosystem type and background climate.
A better understanding of the overall effects and so urces of variation of plant diversity (plant
mixtures compared to the average of constituent monocultures) on pathogens and invertebrate
herbivores could help us formulate plant diversity strategies that not only control pest and
disease outbreaks but also enhance ecosystem functions.

Pathogens and invRertebrate herbivores may be less abundant in more taxonomically,
functionally and phylogenetically diverse plant communities. Compared to two-species mixtures,
those with higher taxonomic diversity (TD) may experience lower abundance of pathogens or
invertebrate herbivores due to the dilution effect 4,5, which makes it harder for specialist
pathogens or invertebrate herbivores to locate their host plants. Associational resistance concepts
also predict that specific plant association may decrease the likelihood of detection by, and/or
vulnerability to, pathogens and herbivores 6,7. However, with the same level of taxonomic
diversity, the abundance and damage of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores may still be
influenced by the extent of trait variation because the physical and chemical traits of plants are
closely related to the susceptibility to pathogens and the feeding preference for invertebrate
herbivores 8-10. More diverse traits can involve different defense mechanisms, growth forms, or
phenologies, which can reduce pathogens or herbivores damage. Although functional diversity
(FD) can explain some aspects of the species trait dissimilarities, these dissimilarities of a large
number of species’ physical and chemical attributes may not be easily measured. In contrast,
phylogenetic diversity (PD) can capture phylogenetically conserved dissimilarity of traits (often
unmeasured) among species 11,12. Thus, we expect that greater FD or PD within plant
communities may reduce the likelihood of shared pathogens or invertebrate herbivores species
among plant species, thereby reducing their accumulation and Sdamage.

The mixture effects on pathogens and invertebraRte herbivores may change with stand age,
ecosystem types (croplands, forests, grasslands, and pots) and background climate. Monocultures
provide high host densities for pathogens or iInvertebrate herbivores, thus promoting the build-up
of these populations over time 13,14, which progressively impairs biomass production 15,16.
Conversely, diverse communities may take time to establish beneficial interactions (e.g.
mutualists, predators of herbivores) and foster more suppressive soil microbiomes that inhibit
pathogens over time 17,18. Thus, we expect that the reduction in pathogens and invertebrate
herbivores in plant mixtures would be more pronounced over time compared to monocultures
due to cumulative effects such as enhanced natural enemy populations and improved plant
health. The responses of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores to plant mixtures could vary
between ecosystem types as a result of differences in vegetation types (e.g. trees vs herbs). For
example, in diverse plant communities, the presence of larger non-host trees in forests as
physical barriers might limit the spread or dispersal of pathogens or invertebrate herbivores more
effectively than the herbaceous species in grasslands 19,20. Furthermore, pathogens and
invertebrate herbivores in warm and humid conditions have higher abundance and activities 21,22
and compete more intensively for specific food resources, causing them to feed on a wider range
of plants 23,24. Therefore, we expect that the decline in pathogens and invertebrate herbivores in plant
mixtures may be less pronounced in warm and humid climates due to the generally higher
activity, reproduction, and survival rates of pathogens and herbivores under such climatic
conditions 25,26.

Previous meta-analyses have reported plant diversity (i.e. species richness or genetic
diversity) reduces plant diseases 27, pathogens damage 28, insect herbivory 29, herbivores
abundance 30, pest abundance 31,32, and positive effects of planSt intraspecific diversity on
arthropods 33. Although these syntheses have advanced Runderstanding of how plant diversity—
primarily species richness, genetic diversity and intraspecific diversity—on average influences
pathogens, and herbivores, it remains unclearI how these influences vary with different
confounding covariates. For example, the effects of diversity may depend on the magnitude of
diversity (e.g. two species versus a higher number of species), other facets of diversity such as
FD and PD, the type of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores (e.g., fungal vs. bacteria; foliar vs.
soil vs. stem; specialists vs. generalists), stand age, and background climate. Moreover, previous
meta-analyses have demonstrated positive effects of plant diversity on productivity 34-37.
However, how these productivity gains are linked to diversity-driven changes in pathogens and
herbivores pressure remains largely unknown at a global scale (but see Beillouin, et al. 38 for
evidence in croplands).

Here, we conduct a global meta-analysis with 2,315 observations of plant mixtures and
constituent monocultures from 316 studies across four ecosystem types (croplands, forests,
grasslands, and pots), to examine how plant taxonomic, functional and phylogenetic diversity
affects the performance (abundance and damage to plants) of pathogens and invertebrate
herbivores to further influence plant productivity (Fig. 1; Supplementary Data 1). To compare
the relative importance of diversity indicators on the same dimension, we employ unified Hill
diversity indices 39. Specifically, we test the following hypotheses: (a) plant mixtures would, on
average, decrease the abundance and damage of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores; (b) the
magnitude of the negative mixture effects would increase with multifaceted diversity (TD, FD,
and PD) in mixtures and stand age, and are less pronounced in warm and humid climates; (c) the
positive mixture effects on plant productivity would be associated with the reduction of the
pathogens and invertebrate herbivores. Here, TD for q = 0 is sSimply species richness, for q = 1, it
is the Shannon index, and for q = 2, it is the Simpson inRdex. The Hill diversity metrics of q = 1
and 2 are influenced by the dominant species that are not biased due to the sample size and are
sufficiently accurate in estimating diversity wIithout the need for rarefaction 40. Hill diversity
metrics with q = 1 including functional diversity (FDq1), phylogenetic diversity (PDq1), and
taxonomic diversity (TDq1) explained greater amounts of variation in our focal measures than
their alternatives (q = 0 and 2) (Table S1; Table S2), hence we focus on them hereafter.

---

## Results

Diversity metrics influences plant mixture effects
For pathogens, compared to monocultures, plant mixtures on average reduced pathogens
abundance and damage by 30.1% (95% confidence intervals, CI, -58.1% – -2.13%) and 31.7%
(CI, -41.7% – -21.7%), respectively (Fig. 2a). The effect of plant mixtures on pathogens damage
was consistently negative across different host specificity (specialists vs. generalists), habitat
(foliar vs. soil vs. stem) and taxonomy (fungal vs. bacteria), with the only exception being
generalist pathogens, for which no significant differences were observed (Fig. 2a). For
invertebrate herbivores, plant mixture on average reduced abundance and damage of invertebrate
herbivores by 21.6% (CI, -28.2% – -15.0%) and 25.1% (CI, -36.2% – -14.0%), respectively.
Similarly, the effect of plant mixtures on herbivores was consistently negative across different
host specificity and habitat except for generalist herbivores (Fig. 2b). Overall, plant mixtures had
higher productivity than the average of corresponding monocultures (Fig. 2).

The negative effects of plant mixture on pathogens performance (abundance and damage
to plants) became more pronounced with increases in all diversity metrics (TDq1, FDq1, PDq1)
in mixtures (Fig. 3a, c, e; Table S3; Fig. S4a). In contrast, the eSffect of plant mixture on
invertebrate herbivores performance (abundance and daRmage to plants) remained non-significant
with TDq1, FDq1 and PDq1 (Fig. 3b, d, f; Table S3; Fig.S4c). Similar results were obtained
when assessing the effect of plant diversity vaIriables at q=0 and q=2 on the performance of
pathogens and invertebrate herbivores (Fig. S2; Fig. S3). When categorizing pathogens and
invertebrate herbivores into specialist and generalist groups, the negative effects of plant
mixtures on specialist pathogens and invertebrate herbivores performance became more
pronounced with increasing TDq1, FDq1 and PDq1 (Fig. 4), while those on generalist pathogen
and invertebrate herbivores showed no significant relationships with any diversity metrics in
mixtures (Fig. 4). When categorizing pathogens and invertebrate herbivores into foliar and soil-
borne groups, plant species mixtures consistently reduced the performance of both foliar and soil
pathogens with increasing TDq1, FDq1 and PDq1 (Fig. S5a, c, e), while their effects on foliar
and soil invertebrate herbivores remained non-significant with TDq1, FDq1 and PDq1 (Fig. S5b,
d, f). TDq1, FDq1 and PDq1 do not significantly influence the effect of plant mixture on stem
pathogens and invertebrate herbivores (Table S7). When categorizing pathogens into fungal and
bacteria, plant mixture effects on fungal pathogens performance decreased with all diversity
metrics in mixtures (Fig. S6).

Stand age influences plant mixture effects
With increasing stand age, plant mixture effects on pathogens performance became more
negative (Fig. 5a; Fig. S4b), while the effects on invertebrate herbivores performance shifted
from negative to positive (Fig. 5b; Fig. S4d), with consistent trends between foliar and soil-borne
groups (Fig. 5e, f). Stand age do not significantly influence the effect of plant mixture on stem
pathogens and invertebrate herbivores (Table S7). The impact Sof stand age on plant mixture
effects on pathogen and invertebrate herbivore performaRnce does not differ between specialists
and generalists (Fig. 5c, d). When categorizing pathogens into fungal and bacteria groups, the
effect of plant mixtures on fungal pathogens dIecreased with stand age, whereas no significant
relationship was observed for bacterial pathogens (Fig. S6b). The effects of plant species
mixtures on pathogens performance were consistently negative across all ecosystem types (Fig.
S7a). The MAT and MAP do not significantly influence the effect of plant mixture on pathogens
and invertebrate herbivores (Table S4; Table S5).

Plant diversity enhances productivity by regulating pathogens and herbivores
The structural equation models based on the 134 studies (169 observations for pathogens,
572 observations for invertebrate herbivores) that simultaneously reported plant mixture effects
on pathogens (or invertebrate herbivores) and plant productivity showed negative associations
between the mixture effects on pathogens (or invertebrate herbivores) and those on productivity
(standardized r = -0.15 for pathogens and r= -0.12 for invertebrate herbivores) (Fig. 6; Fig. S8a,
d). Increasing FDq1 and PDq1, reduced pathogens performance, resulting in positive indirect
effects of FDq1 and PDq1 on plant productivity (r = -0.30 × -0.15 = 0.05 for FDq1 and = -0.35 ×
-0.15 = 0.05 for PDq1, Fig. 6a), while the total effects of FDq1 and PDq1 (r = 0.05 + 0.05 =
0.10) are similar with that of TDq1 (r = -0.60 × -0.18 = 0.11) (Fig. S9a). PDq1 also had a
positive direct effect on productivity (r =0.45, Fig. 6a; Fig. S8b). In addition, mixture effects on
pathogens performance decreased with stand age and those on plant productivity increased with
stand age (Fig. 6a; Fig. S8c). For specialist pathogen, increasing PDq1 and TDq1 reduced
pathogens performance, resulting in their positive indirect effects on plant productivity (r = -0.38
× -0.33 = 0.13 for PDq1 and r = -0.32 × -0.34 = 0.11 for TDq1, Fig. 6b; Fig. S9b). For generalist
pathogens, higher PDq1 also reduced pathogen performance (r = -0.59, Fig. 6c), but it did not
result in statistically significant indirect effects on plant productivity (Fig. 6c). Increasing FDq1,
PDq1 and TDq1 in mixtures did not significantly influence invertebrate herbivores performance
(r = -0.01 for FDq1, r = -0.08 for PDq1 and r= -0.03 for TDq1, Fig. 6d, Fig. S9d). Moreover,
PDq1 had a positive direct effect on productivity (r = 0.21, Fig. 6d; Fig. S8e), and the mixture

stand age (Fig. 6d; Fig. S8f). For specialist invertebrate herbivores, increasing FDq1 and TDq1

Fig. S9e). For generalist invertebrate herbivores, increasing FDq1, PDq1 and TDq1 did not
significantly reduce invertebrate herbivores performance (Fig. 6f, Fig. S9f).

---

## Methods

Data collection
Studies were selected through a search on the Web of Science and the China National
Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI; https://www.cnki.net) (peer-reviewed journal articles until
January 2025) using the Boolean search string 1: AB=((plant diversity OR tree diversity OR crop
diversity OR grass diversity OR plant mix* OR "species diversity" OR “species richness” OR
“species mix*” OR “mixed cult*” OR “pure and mix*”) AND (pathogen* OR pest OR insect
OR herbiv* OR beetle* OR disease OR infect*)) and the Boolean search string 2: AB=((species
diversity OR tree diversity OR plant diversity OR species richness OR species mix* OR mixed
cult* OR crop diversity OR mix* plantation OR pure and mix*) AND (pathogen* OR pest OR
insect OR herbiv* OR disease OR infection) AND (product* OR biomass OR yield OR growth
OR basal area OR volume)). The literature search was performed following guidelines from
PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 57; Fig. S1). In
this study, the term "invertebrate herbivores" refers to organisms that include not only
herbivorous insects but also phytophagous nematodes and mites. To accurately assess the effects
of pathogens and invertebrate herbivores on the diversity-ecosystem productivity relationship,
we reviewed each article to determine whether the studies met the following criteria: (1) the
study was purposely designed to investigate the effects of plant mixture on pathogens,
invertebrate herbivores; (2) the study had at least one plant mixture treatment and corresponding
monocultures; (3) papers focused merely on the effects of diversity on plants without other
trophic level were excluded; (4) studies were purposely implemented to separate the effects of
plant species diversity from other factors, such as water treatment and nutrition addition.

When different publications included the same data from one study, we recorded the data
only once. When a study included plant mixtures of different numbers of species, we considered
them distinct observations. Also, when a publication included several experiments under
different abiotic conditions, such as different locations, treatments, stand age and ecosystem
type, we considered them different observations. We used WebPlotDigitizer
(https://automeris.io/WebPlotDigitizer) to digitally extract data from figures when the results
were graphically reported. We obtained a meta-dataset of 2,315 observations from 316 studies
that involved the mixing of live plants in croplands (155 studies), forests (95 studies with 8 in
natural forests and 87 in plantations), grasslands (43 studies) and pots (26 studies) (Fig. 1;
Supplementary Data 1, Supplementary Note 1).

We obtained plant species name, species richness, the species proportions in plant
mixtures, plant productivity, abundance and damage of pathogens or invertebrate herbivores,
geographical location (latitude, longitude, and altitude), ecosystem type, stand age (SA), the
types of pathogens (fungal vs. bacteria; foliar vs. soil vs. stem; specialists vs. generalists) and
invertebrate herbivores (foliar vs. soil vs. stem; specialists vs. generalists) from original
publications (Supplementary Data 1). Due to data limitations, we followed the approach of
previous meta-analyses 35,36 and used a range of proxy variables—including biomass,
production, height, cover, yield, and volume—to represent productivity. These metrics are all
measures or proxies of primary productivity and can thus be collectively analyzed, in contrast to
secondary productivity, which reflects energy conversion by heterotrophs. This allowed us to
include a broader set of studies and observations. We used the initial plant density of each species in
forests, grasslands, croplands and pot experiments to calculate the species proportions in the
species mixtures. Similar to previous studies 58, SA was recorded as the number of years since
the establishment of the stand/pot experiment. For those studies conducted under natural climates
including croplands, forests and grasslands, we obtained mean annual temperature (MAT) and
mean annual precipitation (MAP) for each study site from original publications; when
unavailable, it was derived based on geographic locations using the WorldClim version 2 dataset
59.

We categorized pathogens and invertebrate herbivores as specialists or generalists based on
the classifications provided in the original literature sources. Specialist pathogens or invertebrate
herbivores are species that feed on a specific type of plant or a narrow range of related plants,
usually confined to a single family or genus. In contrast, generalist pathogens or invertebrate
herbivores can feed on a wide variety of plants spanning multiple families 60. The dataset on
pathogens included 42 studies on specialists and 11 on generalists. Invertebrate herbivores
included 36 studies on specialists and 38 on generalists. Most studies focused on fungal
pathogens (74 studies), with only 9 studies addressing bacteria pathogens. We gathered data
from 51 studies on foliar pathogens and 33 on soil pathogens, 4 on stem pathogens, as well as
213 studies on foliar invertebrate herbivores, 31 on soil invertebrate herbivores and 10 on stem
invertebrate herbivores (Fig. 2). Previous studies indicated that an increase in the abundance of
pathogens and invertebrate herbivores was positively correlated with their damage to plants 61,62.
Thus, we refer to the abundance and damage caused by pathogens or invertebrate herbivores as
their performance, following the terminology used by Wan et al. 9,30.

Functional and phylogenetic diversity quantification
Our dataset includes a total of 514 plant species, comprising 151 crops, 136 grasses, and
229 woody plants. We obtained species mean trait values for the specific leaf area (SLA), leaf N
(Nmass), root diameter (RD) and specific root length (SRRL) from the TRY Plant Trait Database
63, Botanical Information and Ecology Network (BIEN) Database 64, Global Inventory of Floras
and Traits (GIFT) Database 65, Community Responses to Resource Experiments (CoRRE)
Database 66, Fine-Root Ecology Database (FRED) 67 and the Global Root Traits (GRooT)
Database 68. These plant traits are among the most frequently measured and have been previously
reported to be related to pathogens infection 69,70 or feeding by invertebrate herbivores 48,71.
When trait data were unavailable in the above database, we obtained them from published data
sets and literature (131 species).

We used Hill numbers to quantify taxonomic diversity (TD), functional diversity (FD) and
phylogenetic diversity (PD) through the iNEXT.3D standardisation with iNEXT.3D package 40.
The Hill numbers provide a unified and comparable framework for measuring biodiversity across
these three dimensions. We obtained the phylogenetic tree via the phylo.maker function from the
V. PhyloMaker package and then calculate the values of TD, FD and PD using the ObsAsy3D
function from the iNEXT.3D package. In this study, FD was calculated based on leaf and root
traits, including SLA, Nmass, RD and SRL. Our sensitive analysis showed that FD calculated

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In their study, Huang and colleagues sought to show how plant diversity can reduce damage from insect pests and fungal pathogens, and how this associational resistance (a key concept in this field, e.g. Barbosa et al. 2099, but never cited by the authors) translates into gains in primary productivity. To do this, they used a meta-analysis. Each of these plant diversity response variables (resistance and productivity) has already been the subject of many meta-analyses, and it is surprising that they are not cited in the introduction or discussion. For example, for the effect of plant diversity on pest damage, among many others: Beillouin et al. 2021; Jactel et al. 2021; Hahn et al. 2024; Yousefi et al. 2024. See also the recent meta-analysis by Field et al. 2025 on pathogens. For the effect on productivity, again these are just several examples in forests: Warner et al. 2023; Jactel et al. 2018; Zhang et al. 2012. This should be acknowledged and, above all, one should avoid saying in the introduction that the results of the studies are inconsistent. In hundreds of cases, it is clear that some effects will be positive, others negative, others neutral. It is precisely the role of meta-analyses to highlight the direction (the sign) of the overall mean effect size.
More original is the authors' attempt to link the effect of plant diversity on pest damage with its effect on the productivity of the same plants. The problem is that the methodology employed is too flawed to produce reliable and convincing results. I list the problems below in the order in which the methods are described in the manuscript.
1. Data collection: I'm familiar with the bibliography used for forestry, and I'm sure that in many cases the combination of keywords (product* OR biomass OR yield) would not have found them. 23 articles on forest insects were selected, whereas the meta-analysis by Jactel et al. 2021 is based on 69 articles (3 times as many). 9 articles deal with forest pathogens, whereas the meta-analysis by Field et al. 2025 uses 44 (5 times more). These discrepancies are significant and raise the question of the exhaustiveness of the bibliographic search.
2. Functional diversity: the inclusion of root traits is interesting in itself, but none of the insect pests or pathogens cited for the forest cases are present in the soil. The functional diversity index is therefore not relevant for testing the effects on damage reported in the selected publications.
3. Calculating effect size: this is one of the most important methodological problems in the manuscript. With regard to effect size for pest damage, the calculation of Xc is unclear, as 1) it is not clear why a sum (Sigma) should be used and 2) multiplying an average damage in the monoculture by the proportion of the species in the mixture does not work if, for example, the damage is expressed in %. As far as the effect size for productivity is concerned, the Xc formula is similarly unclear, and in particular which (i) effects are to be summed. More importantly, the simple ratio of tree sizes is not sufficient to estimate productivity. Primary productivity corresponds to the increase in volume or biomass over a given time step. To calculate productivity, you therefore need to have data on the volume or above-ground biomass (AGB) of trees at two dates and calculate the difference, divided by the number of years between two measurements. This is not done here.
4. Calculating effect size: there is also an inconsistency in L395-396, where it is stated that there is no significant difference in the effect of diversity between specialist and generalist herbivores, whereas table S5 shows the opposite.
5. Relative contribution of diversity metrics on productivity: this is undoubtedly the major problem with the study. Correlation does not mean causality. In the SEM, the direction of the downward arrow from pest performance to productivity implies that the reduction in damage inflicted on plants would explain (in part) the increase in their productivity. But it's just as possible that the increase in plant productivity explains the reduced damage inflicted by herbivores or pathogens. Indeed, there are numerous studies showing that more vigorous plants, i.e. those with stronger growth, are more resistant to attacks by pests, particularly secondary pests. The role of associational resistance is therefore by no means demonstrated by this model. To do so would require more complicated studies, such as monitoring plant growth over several years after a severe pest attack followed by an absence of attack, or manipulating herbivory intensity. Here, at best, the SEM model should use a two-way arrow between pest performance and productivity (but we have seen the limits of calculating this productivity), and the discussion should seek to understand the common or pleiotropic effects of plant diversity rather than its cascading effects.
For these various methodological reasons, I don't think this manuscript can be accepted for publication without a major revision.
